item.title: Superfund: EPA Should Collect and Use Information on the Effectiveness of Its Recovery of Cleanup Costs
item.description:
What GAO Found
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) uses the Hazardous Substance Superfund Trust Fund to finance cleanup costs at Superfund sites where responsible parties cannot be found or cannot pay. In fiscal years 2006 through 2024, the Trust Fund received about $34 billion in constant 2024 dollars, mostly from General Fund transfers. Congress appropriated about $32.8 billion from the Trust Fund for the Superfund program over this period. Revenue from the reinstated Superfund taxes provided substantial funds for the program in fiscal year 2024. In fiscal years 1996 through 2024, the time frame for which reliable data were available, EPA spent about $25.8 billion at nonfederal National Priorities List (NPL) sites. Remedial activities were the largest category, accounting for about half of EPA’s expenditures at these sites.
Through its efforts to hold potentially responsible parties accountable for cleanup, EPA has identified at least one such party for most nonfederal NPL sites, according to EPA data. However, EPA has faced challenges recovering costs. Challenges include having fewer experienced potentially responsible party search staff over the last 10 to 15 years and a limited ability to hold such parties liable. GAO estimates that in fiscal years 1996 through 2024, EPA recovered less than half of what it spent at nonfederal NPL sites.
EPA Expenditures and Amounts Recovered from Potentially Responsible Parties at Nonfederal NPL Sites, Fiscal Years 1996–2024
Note: Deleted sites are those where cleanup is complete. This analysis includes 1,622 National Priorities List (NPL) sites and expenditures from the Superfund Trust Fund. It is a point-in-time estimate since cost recovery efforts are ongoing, according to EPA officials.
EPA has established some Superfund performance goals and measures to ensure it takes timely cost recovery steps but does not have such tools to assess the effectiveness of its cost recovery across nonfederal NPL sites. EPA officials said they have not done this because cost recovery is a continuous process that may take years to complete. However, measuring the effectiveness of its cost recovery performance—such as by region—would allow EPA to determine how much of the billions of dollars in cleanup costs it is recovering and what kinds of efforts work best to successfully recover costs. This would help EPA determine resource needs and target enforcement efforts.
Why GAO Did This Study
The Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act of 1980, as amended, established the Superfund program to address sites with hazardous substances. Hazardous substances found at Superfund sites have been linked to a variety of human health and environmental problems. The program is administered by EPA, which lists the most contaminated sites on the NPL.
Superfund site cleanups are often expensive and lengthy. EPA funds cleanups when it cannot identify parties responsible for the contamination, or when such parties fail to act. The Trust Fund was primarily financed by revenue from Superfund taxes until they expired in 1995. In 2021, Congress began reinstating some Superfund taxes.
GAO was asked to review EPA funding, expenditures, and cost recovery at nonfederal NPL sites. This report examines, among other things, (1) funding that the Trust Fund and Superfund program received; (2) amounts EPA spent at nonfederal NPL sites; and (3) the extent to which EPA has identified potentially responsible parties, recovered cleanup costs, and assessed the effectiveness of its cost recovery efforts.
GAO analyzed EPA and budget data, visited Superfund sites, and interviewed EPA officials.
